A document presented yesterday afternoon by the conference presidency calls for keeping the projected exceedance of the 1.5-degree threshold as brief and minimal as possible. Unlike in the earlier draft, a phase-out of fossil fuels is no longer mentioned. Panama has threatened to block a consensus decision if it does not include more ambitious commitments to climate protection. Decisions must be adopted by consensus among all nations. An extension of the summit is therefore considered likely. TAGS COP31 Facebook X WhatsApp Email Print UN Bonn Contact Terms of Use Fraud Alert FAQ Privacy Notice Copyright United Nations 2026

Nearly 200 nations are deadlocked after two weeks of grinding negotiations in Turkiye with feuds over energy, science and finance tipped to drag into the weekend. A closing session was convened late Friday well past the summit’s official closing time but only to approve technical matters as the wider political deal eluded negotiators. READ ALSO: COP31 draft deal calls for ‘accelerated action’ to exit fossil fuels “We’ve been negotiating for days to find the common ground. We have made great progress… But the world is still hopeful and waits for good news from this room,” COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is Turkiye’s environment minister, told the plenary. Midway through his speech, Kurum was forced to pause while a protester shouted “You are killing the future!” before being escorted from the hall. Expectations of a major breakthrough have been low at COP31 as countries grapple with an oil price shock and geopolitical tensions stemming from the war in Iran. The summit follows a string of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Nepal and Indonesia and unfolds as a super El Nino pattern amplifies the risk of further extreme weather. COP31 co-host Australia unveiled a draft deal earlier this week calling for a faster phaseout of fossil fuels, a flashpoint at UN climate talks where producers have fiercely resisted such calls. A second, pared-down draft released on Thursday stripped away all mentions of fossil fuels — sending negotiators rushing back to the bargaining table. The European Union said the revised draft “risks turning this climate COP into a fossil summit”. A dozen European and developing countries — from France to Panama and the Solomon Islands — released a letter Friday insisting that the deal include “a clear transition away from fossil fuels”. Panama, which also signed the letter, threatened to walk away from the talks. The country’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, is a vocal critic of the climate talks where he accuses a “petroleum mafia” of blocking progress. A third draft is expected Satu

r as long as it takes, to get the job done”. “People have strong views, of course — I am not stepping away from that. But no one has said to me, ‘let’s give up and go home’,” the veteran of five COPs said. Brazil’s national secretary for climate change, Aloisio Lopes Pereira de Melo, summed up the mood in Antalya: “At this point, no one is happy,” he told reporters. The draft “cover decision” proposes a target to electrify the global economy — a push to replace technologies that burn fossil fuels directly, like diesel cars and gas heating, with electric alternatives. The goal is championed by COP31 hosts Turkiye and Australia who tout “electrification” as integral to tackling concerns over energy security and sluggish global progress in cutting heat-trapping emissions. “Electrification is the key to transitioning away from fossil fuels,” said Bowen, who is chairing the negotiations. The proposal calls for countries to boost the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35 percent by 2035. But it does not specify that the additional electricity must come from renewables rather than coal or gas, spurring some countries to demand an explicitly “clean” target. Some countries also rejected a proposal to ramp up carbon capture, dismissing it as a costly, unproven technology that could allow polluters to keep burning fossil fuels. “We’re quite disappointed by the text,” Vanuatu’s Climate Minister Ralph Regenvanu told AFP . “We want to see the references to false solu

. Negotiations are also deadlocked over long-running complaints by developing countries that rich nations are falling short in their obligations to help them confront climate change. “We didn’t come here to beg,” said Ghana’s environment minister, Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings. “The (African) continent will not accept an outcome that offers declarations without the resources to deliver them,” she said. australia france European Union UN Iran Europe climate change indonesia Ghana Nepal Africa global warming fossil fuels IPCC Solomon Islands Turkiye Panama nations World countries Antalya Murat Kurum COP31 Chris Bowen COP31 climate summit Juan Carlos Navarro Aloisio Lopes Pereira de Melo Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings Ralph Regenvanu UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Comments 200 characters remaining More Stories Bilawal hopes PM Shehbaz completes five-year term; calls for engagement with Imran's party Govt slashes petrol price by Re1, raises diesel's Rs2 per litre Indian man sentenced to more than 19 years in US for plotting to kill Sikh separatist Saudi-led forces strike port to ‘destroy’ Houthi capabilities Pakistan rejects undiplomatic, irresponsible remarks of India at UN OGDCL, PPL and PARCO scrap LPG auctions in face of LHC challenge Improving debt sustainability: FD report says outlook remains vulnerable 25 federal institutions: Govt identifies misuse of public funds and abuse of authority FCC releases detailed verdict on provincial infrastructure cess 16.219m connections in 5 DISCOs: I
